section_heading: CPF refund when selling or transferring property > IMPORTANT NOTE:
content: To reduce the amount you need to refund when you sell your property, consider **making voluntary housing refunds**. Voluntary housing refunds allows you to enjoy the attractive interest rates of your CPF savings.

section_heading: Retain $20,000 in your OA if you are taking a housing loan > Notice
content:
CPF members who purchase an HDB flat and take an HDB loan can choose to retain up to $20,000 in their Ordinary Account (OA), with the remainder going towards their housing loan payment.

Buyers taking a bank loan can choose to retain any amount of their OA savings.

These funds\* provide a safety net for you to pay your monthly instalments during unforeseen circumstances, such as a temporary loss of income.

\* You can also build more emergency funds in your OA by using cash to pay for part or all of your monthly instalments, or making a voluntary housing refund.

This sum of money will provide greater convenience to be used for emergency housing needs as compared to liquidating fixed deposits which may result in interest losses due to early withdrawal.

In addition, your OA savings earn risk-free interest of 2.5% annually, which allows you to accumulate more funds in your OA for future retirement or housing needs.

\*Additional 1% is paid on the first $60,000 across all CPF accounts, which is capped at $20,000 for the OA. It will first be credited to the RA or SA.

The OA savings retained may earn an additional 1% interest, which is used to build your Special Account (SA) or Retirement Account (RA) savings and better prepare you for retirement. It can also be transferred to the SA or RA to earn up to 6% interest subjected to the prevailing limits.

You must decide how much (up to $20,000) to retain in your OA at the point of purchase. For more details, please visit the HDB site.

The remainder of your OA savings after retaining up to $20,000 will be used to pay for the down payment of your flat before HDB disburses your housing loan.

section_heading: Protecting against losing your home > Notice
content:
HPS is for CPF members who own an HDB flat and are paying their monthly housing instalments using CPF savings or cash. It insures members until he/she turns 65, or until the housing loans are paid up.

Should your housing loan only be paid up after you turn 65, do consider getting private insurance coverage after your HPS cover ends at 65.

HPS does not cover private residential properties, such as executive condominiums (ECs) or privatised Housing and Urban Development Company (HUDC) flats.

If you’ve an outstanding housing loan for a private property, consider purchasing private insurance coverage.

If you’re using CPF savings to pay your monthly housing instalments, HPS is required. If you’re using cash, we strongly encourage you to apply.

Your eligibility for an HPS cover is subject to approval and you being in good health. You may be required to undergo a medical examination. We may also request a copy of the medical report from your attending doctor.

If you’re not eligible for HPS cover, you can still use your CPF savings to pay your monthly housing instalments.

Rest assured that in the event of a claim, HPS will settle the outstanding housing loan, up to the insured sum, with HDB or the mortgagee directly.

Protect your home with one of the lowest premiums on the market.

Payment is simple, with annual premiums deducted automatically from your Ordinary Account (OA).

Any HPS cover issued based on false or misleading information can be voided at any time, and such insurance claims will be denied. In such situations, any premiums paid will not be refunded.

section_heading: Protecting against losing your home > Notice
content:
Your share of the HPS cover should at least match the proportion of the monthly housing instalment which is payable with your CPF savings and/or cash. The total share of cover per household should add up to at least 100%.

Also, you and your co-owner(s) can each choose to insure for a higher share of cover, for up to 100% per owner. In the event of a claim, HPS will settle the outstanding housing loan up to the insured sum, based on the share of cover applied.

As a higher share of cover results in a higher annual premium being deducted from your OA, be sure to consider your future retirement needs when deciding the share of cover.

Use our HPS Premium Calculator to estimate your HPS premium, based on your decided share of cover.

Ensure that you’ve enough funds in your OA for premium payments on your policy anniversary month.

Keep in mind that your cover could lapse if you fall behind on your premium payments. You’ll need to apply to join HPS again with your eligibility subject to your health condition at the point of reapplication.

If you’re taking an HDB loan, you can apply for HPS the same time you apply to withdraw your CPF savings for monthly housing instalments through HDB.

If you’re taking a bank loan, you can submit an online application to apply for HPS.

You can submit an online application to apply for HPS.

Your annual premium will be automatically deducted from your OA. We’ll inform you to top up your OA if the balance is not enough to pay the premium.

Alternatively, family members (i.e. your spouse/parent/child/sibling) who co-own the flat with you, can authorise us to use their OA savings to pay your HPS premium shortfall.

section_heading: Protecting against losing your home > Notice
content:
Adjust your HPS cover to ensure that you’re adequately covered.

If you’ve used your CPF savings to repay the loan (for both HDB and bank loans), there is no need to apply to adjust your HPS cover. We’ll automatically adjust your HPS cover if the loan quantum and/or repayment period is reduced. We’ll notify you for HPS cover adjustment if the loan quantum and/or repayment is increased.

If you’ve refinanced your housing loan and are already covered under HPS, you do not need to apply as your HPS cover will automatically be adjusted.

If you’re taking a bank loan and have used cash to repay the loan, or changed the loan repayment period, you can submit an online application to adjust your HPS cover.

When doing so, ensure that your new share of HPS cover is sufficient to pay your share of the outstanding loan in the event of a claim.

You can submit an online application to adjust your HPS cover.

Your HPS cover will be terminated when you:

- Sell your HDB flat
- Fully repay your housing loan, or
- Have a new HPS insurance cover issued to you for your new flat.

For HDB loans

If you fully repaid your HDB housing loan, you do not need to inform us, regardless of whether you used CPF savings or cash. Your HPS cover will be automatically terminated.

For bank loans

If you fully repaid your bank loan using CPF savings, you do not need to inform us. Your HPS cover will be automatically terminated.

If you fully repaid your bank loan using cash, your HPS cover will not be automatically terminated. You must write to us to terminate your HPS cover.

section_heading: Protecting against losing your home > Notice
content:
Your Single Premium cover will insure you until you turn 55 or 60 years old. Find out when it will be converted to an Annual Premium HPS cover. You'll be able to continue enjoying insurance protection and use your CPF savings for monthly housing instalments.

You can apply for HPS exemption if you’ve the following insurance policies:

- Whole Life
- Term Life
- Endowments
- Life Riders (must be attached to a basic policy)
- Mortgage Reducing Term Assurance (MRTA) / Decreasing Term Rider

These policies must cover your outstanding housing loan up to the full term of loan or until you turn 65, whichever is earlier.

Doing so will avoid any delay in commencing the use of your CPF savings for your monthly housing instalments.

You can apply for HPS exemption after you have obtained legal ownership of the flat and the housing loan for the property has been disbursed.

If you have not previously used your CPF savings for your HDB flat at the time of purchase or for your monthly housing instalment, please fill up this application form to start using your CPF savings for your HDB flat.

Please approach the insurer(s) of your private insurance policy(s) to submit your application to be exempted from HPS. We will only process applications submitted through insurers.

You will need to provide your insurer(s) with supporting documents showing your current\* housing loan details, i.e. loan commencement date, balance loan amount, balance term of loan & the mortgage rate. These can generally be found on your housing loan statement.

\*Within 6 months from the date the application for exemption is submitted.

section_heading: Protecting against losing your home > Notice
content:
If you are covered under HPS and we receive your HPS exemption request from your insurer within one month of the issuance of your HPS cover, we will refund the full premium into your Ordinary Account. Otherwise, you will receive a pro-rated premium refund upon the termination of your HPS cover.

You can make an HPS claim in the event of death, terminal illness, or total permanent disability.

section_heading: Claiming under the Home Protection Scheme
content:
If the insured member has an outstanding housing loan, we will automatically assess the deceased’s claim eligibility once CPF Board is notified of the member’s death by the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA).

CPF Board will inform the co-owner(s) or next-of-kin of the outcome and if additional information is required.

When the claim is approved, the outstanding loan will be paid directly to the mortgagee.

Terminal illness refers to an illness that is likely to result in the death of the member within 12 months.

A claim under terminal illness can be made only if the terminal illness started on or after 1 May 2016.

Total permanent disability refers to (i) the inability to take part in any employment permanently, or (ii) the total permanent loss of physical functions of both eyes, or two limbs, or one eye and one limb.

To qualify for a claim under (i), the member must no longer be physically employed.

A claim under (ii) can be made only if the total permanent loss of physical function started on or after 1 May 2016.

Please note the following exclusions before submitting an HPS claim.

HPS claims will not be payable if they arise from excluded pre-existing health conditions stated in the HPS certificate.

HPS claims are not payable if:

- Member has committed self-inflicted injury or suicide.
- Member has committed a criminal offence punishable by death.
- The claim arose out of the member's own intentional criminal act.

HPS claims are not payable if:

- Member provided false or misleading information.
- The claim arose from wars, warlike operations, or participation in any riot.

section_heading: Claiming under the Home Protection Scheme
content:
The HPS claim benefits will be paid to the Housing and Development Board (HDB) or the mortgagee directly to settle the outstanding housing loan (based on the share of HPS cover) up to the sum insured.

If the HPS sum assured is higher than the outstanding loan, the excess amount will be paid to the insured member's CPF Ordinary Account.

For claims under death grounds, HPS benefits will be paid in a lump sum.

Any excess claim amounts will be paid to the insured member's CPF Ordinary Account. Thereafter, the deceased member’s CPF savings will be distributed to nominees. In cases where no nominations are made, they will be distributed by the Public Trustee under the intestacy laws or Muslim inheritance laws.

Co-owners or personal representatives will be informed once the HPS claim payment has been made.

For claims under medical grounds, the member's housing instalments can be paid by HPS for up to two years. After this period, the member’s eligibility to claim the remaining insured amount in a lump sum will be reviewed.

Any excess claim amounts will be paid to the insured member's CPF Ordinary Account.

section_heading: Single Premium Home Protection Scheme cover > Notice
content:
Members insured under the HPS before 1 March 2001 are covered under the Single Premium until they turn 55 or 60, depending on when they joined the scheme. The maximum cover age is stated on the Single Premium certificate issued to members when their Single Premium covers commence. Single Premium premiums are paid in a lump sum.

Annual Premium covers are issued from 1 March 2001 and cover members until they turn 65. Members under Annual Premium pay their premiums annually.

Your Single Premium (SP) HPS may be converted to an Annual Premium (AP) HPS if there are any changes to your loan repayment period or loan amount, including refinancing of an existing loan. However, any consequential increase to your HPS cover, e.g. increase in cover period or sum assured, is subject to you being in good health. You will remain insured under your SP cover if you are not eligible for the additional AP cover.

If you’re covered under Single Premium cover at age 55 or 60, it’ll be converted to an Annual Premium cover if you still have an outstanding loan.

Your Single Premium cover will end at either age 55 or 60. The Annual Premium cover continues the insurance protection until you turn 65 or your housing loan is fully paid, whichever comes first.

If you’re insured under the new Annual Premium scheme, you can continue to use your CPF savings to pay monthly instalments even after your Single Premium cover has ended.

When you convert from a Single Premium to an Annual Premium cover, you must pay an annual premium for the cover extension and subsequent renewal of your Annual Premium cover.

The new Annual Premium cover is based on the outstanding housing loan amount when your Single Premium cover ends.

section_heading: Single Premium Home Protection Scheme cover > Notice
content:
Get exempted from the Annual Premium scheme if you already have an equivalent private life insurance that covers your outstanding housing loan.

If you’re not using your CPF savings to pay monthly housing instalments and no longer need the financial protection, you can apply to end your Annual Premium cover.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55
content:
Are you thinking of selling your current flat and upgrading to another? Before doing so, do consider:

- Why are you upgrading your flat?
- Is upgrading your best option?

If you have determined that you need to upgrade:

- Are you eligible to do so?
- Should you buy or sell your flat first?
- What type of flats can you go for?
- What locations do you want to live in?
- Case study: Do you have sufficient savings for retirement?

Upgrade to a new home while keeping within your means.

To make prudent financial decisions, consider:

- How much do you need for your next flat?
- How is your loan quantum determined?
- Cash payments
- Type of housing loans available
- Should you use cash, CPF or both cash and CPF to finance your home?

Learn more about the steps involved:

- Process of buying a new/resale flat
- Process of selling your current flat
- Types of ownership: Joint Tenancy vs Tenancy-in-common
- CPF refund process

After purchasing your home, how can you better secure your retirement?

Learn more about:

- Voluntary Housing Refund

Before deciding to buy a larger or more costly flat, it's important to determine why you're doing so and if upgrading is the only option.

For some, you could be looking for a bigger living space, a preferred location, a form of property investment or even an 'upgrade' in lifestyle. However, every choice comes with trade-offs and careful planning is required to ensure that upgrading does not compromise your retirement needs.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55
content:
An important question to ask yourself is whether your reason for upgrading is worth the costs and risks that come with it. Consider if you have the means to do so after you have fully evaluated the implications.

Banks now offer home loans linked to the Singapore Overnight Rate Average (SORA). It's important to be aware that the 3-month compounded SORA are currently at elevated levels.

What this means for you is the potential for an increase in your monthly housing loan payments over time. It is of paramount importance to exercise added prudence when considering borrowing and to maintain an emergency fund as a safeguard against unforeseen circumstances in the current interest rate environment. Additionally, it is crucial to approach new financial commitments with caution.

It is important to evaluate whether the benefits of upgrading outweigh the costs of upgrading since you will need to pay for renovation costs and other expenses such as stamp duty and legal fees on top of the cost of buying the flat.

For instance, if your intention of upgrading is to move closer to your child's school, you may want to consider alternatives such as school bus or student care arrangements before resorting to buying a new flat.

If you have assessed that upgrading is necessary, you should first determine your eligibility.

Have you hit the Minimum Occupation Period(MOP)?

The MOP is the minimum time period that you are required to physically occupy your flat before you can sell it in the open market.

Whether you're purchasing the flat alone or with your family, there are different eligibility conditions and schemes. For example, you must be a Singaporean Citizen aged 35 and above to purchase a flat alone.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55
content:
Whether you buy or sell your flat first, it comes with unavoidable risks and costs. Be it having to look for temporary lodging, or the reduced cash flow when purchasing your next flat, there are uncertainties involved.

- You have a place to move into first
- However, do note:
  - You have to sell your current flat within 6 months of purchasing your new flat
  - You may have a reduced cash flow as you will not have the sales proceeds from your existing flat

- It may take a few months before you sell your flat in the open market
- You may need temporary accommodation during this period which adds to the costs. Here are some options you can consider:
  - Renting an apartment/bedroom
  - Staying at your relative's/parents' place

Do note that whether you buy your next flat or sell your existing one first, the Loan- to-Value limits remain the same i.e., up to 75% for both HDB loan and bank loan.

Find out what homes are well within your budget, to ensure that you can comfortably pay off your home loan without putting a strain on other aspects of your life, especially your future retirement.

Check:

- Condition of flat
- Remaining lease of flat and whether it can last the youngest buyer till age 95

See what flats are available:

Every year, there are several launches of BTO projects in both mature and non-mature estates. BTO projects tend to have a longer waiting time of 3 to 5 years on the average.

Check out HDB's portal for new flats

There will also be flats built in prime, central locations under the Prime Location Housing (PLH) scheme.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55
content:
For completed sale of balance flats, you can collect your keys within 3 months. For those under construction, the wait time for collection depends on the stage of construction.

These are balance flats from past SBF launches which are announced by HDB from time to time.

You can apply for such flats anytime throughout the year.

Similar to SBF, you can collect your keys within 3 months for completed flats. For those under construction, the wait time for collection depends on the stage of construction.

There are many different residential estates in Singapore, each with a unique flavour of its own. Estates are classified into mature or non-mature estates. In general, flats in non-mature estates are more affordable than those in mature estates. However, this phenomenon may change with the times.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Mature Estates
content: Ang Mo Kio, Bedok, Bishan, Bukit Merah, Bukit Timah, Central Area, Clementi, Geylang, Kallang/Whampoa, Marine Parade, Pasir Ris, Queenstown, Serangoon, Tampines, Toa Payoh

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
Bukit Batok, Bukit Panjang, Choa Chu Kang, Hougang, Jurong East, Jurong West, Punggol, Sembawang, Sengkang, Woodlands, Yishun

- Access to mature estates are prioritised for special groups such as first-timer families.
- Mature estates are generally more expensive. For example, in previous BTO exercises, the starting selling price (excluding grants) of a 3-room flat in non-mature estates such as Choa Chu Kang was more than 30% cheaper than a 3-room flat in mature estates such as Kallang. It is important to note that the prices can fluctuate over time and may be influenced by various factors such as market conditions.

If you have decided that upgrading is necessary for you, why not consider living near your children or your parents?

Besides the convenience and being surrounded by your loved ones, you also get to enjoy housing grants and schemes provided by the Government to encourage families to live closer together. These include the Proximity Housing Grant (PHG), as well as other schemes like the Multi-Generation Priority Scheme (MGPS).

There are some regions which will be benefitting from significant development over the next few years, with some already underway. Many of the non-mature estates can be found in these regions. Explore their regional highlights below.

There are exciting plans to develop these urban areas into the Punggol Digital District and the Jurong Lake District, creating vibrant communities for living and working.

More families in the North can look forward to new green and blue spaces to live, work and play at.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
Learn more about the upcoming plans and developments:

The North-East region will see new housing options in the area. Residents across generations will also get to enjoy new facilities and a fresh environment with a range of community amenities, alongside the wealth of greenery and waterways being developed at Buangkok, Punggol and Fernvale.

Learn more about the upcoming plans and developments:

The West side remains Singapore's largest manufacturing hub. There are upcoming plans to bring about an improved working and living environment for everyone.

Residents can look forward to new employment, recreation and leisure opportunities in areas such as Tengah and Jurong Lake District.

Check out the new flats in these areas which may be more affordable as well.

Learn more about the upcoming plans and developments:

In the 2023 national day rally, an important announcement was made regarding the three categories of flats in Singapore's housing market. The three categories are Standard, Plus, and Prime, each offering varying benefits and restrictions to potential homeowners.

Standard flats form the bulk of the housing supply and are subject to standard subsidies and restrictions, which are applied uniformly to all BTO flats.

Plus flats, a newly introduced category, offer a more attractive option as they are located in choicer locations within each region across Singapore, such as near MRT stations and town centres. These flats come with additional subsidies compared to Standard BTO flats, but they also have tighter restrictions.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
Prime flats, on the other hand, are situated in the choicest locations within Singapore, typically closer to the city centre. They offer the highest subsidies among the three categories. However, these flats come with the strictest conditions to ensure they are allocated to those who truly need them. It's important to note that Prime flats are currently offered under the PLH (Prime Location Public Housing) model.

Learn about how James' and Mary's decision today will eventually impact the amount of monthly payouts they receive in their golden years

It is important to buy a home that you can afford and adopt the right mortgage repayment strategy so that you can preserve savings in your Ordinary Account for your retirement.

When you first purchase your home, you have to make some upfront payments and take a loan to finance the remainder of the payment.

There are different ways to finance your home. They include using grants, loans, your Ordinary Account savings and your cash savings, including the sales proceeds from your existing flat.

Your Ordinary Account savings can be used for the downpayment and monthly instalments.

However, there are limits to the amount of Ordinary Account savings you can use for your property. Use the Housing Usage calculator to estimate the amount.

Some expenses cannot be paid with Ordinary Account savings as well.

You can use cash to pay your downpayment and housing loan.

Second-time home buyers are eligible for grants as well. These include:

- Step-up CPF Housing Grant
- Fresh Start Housing Grant
- Proximity Housing Grant

Housing grants obtained are usually credited to the applicant's Ordinary Account after the booking of flat. Housing grants can generally only be used for the downpayment, to offset the purchase price.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
The quantum of upfront payment you have to make depends on the loan quantum you can take. The loan quantum also depends on the type of loan you choose to take, as well as your Loan-to-Value amount, total debt servicing ratio, mortgage servicing ratio and loan tenure.

Learn the implications of these terms to make a more informed decision.

The total debt servicing ratio (TDSR) refers to the portion of a borrower’s gross monthly income that goes towards repaying the monthly debt obligations, including the loan being applied for. A borrower's TDSR should be less than or equal to 55%.

E.g., If your combined monthly income is $8,000, you can use up to $4,400(55%) for your total monthly debt repayment. If you have other loan obligations such as a car loan of $1500, your monthly instalment for your home will be capped at up to $2,900.

The mortgage servicing ratio (MSR) refers to the portion of a borrower’s gross monthly income that goes towards repaying property loans, also known as monthly instalments (MI).

The MSR is capped at 30% of a borrower's gross monthly income. To be prudent, we recommend capping the MI amount at 25% of your monthly income. Do note that MSR applies only to housing loans for the purchase of a HDB flat, or an executive condominium\*.

E.g., If your combined monthly income is $8,000, the maximum monthly instalment allowed is $2,400(30%).

The Loan-to-Value (LTV) limit determines the maximum amount an individual can borrow from a financial institution for a housing loan.

The LTV limit depends on the number of outstanding home loans you have and the loan tenure.

A lower LTV would mean that members have to finance more of their downpayment using either CPF or cash savings.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
The loan tenure is the duration which you are given to repay your loan.

With all things held constant, a shorter loan tenure can mean higher monthly instalments but lower interest paid in total. While a longer loan tenure may lower your monthly instalment, you may end up incurring higher interest expenses in total.

*\*Where the minimum occupation period of the executive condominium has not expired*

When a resale flat is sold above HDB's valuation, the price above the market valuation is known as Cash Over Valuation (COV).

Some things to note:

- You cannot use your Ordinary Account monies to pay for the COV and can only use cash.
- As HDB's valuation is only obtained after the seller and buyer agrees on the price, you may wish to estimate the price carefully and determine your budget before agreeing on the purchase price.

Resale levy is paid when you subsequently purchase a second subsidised flat.

Do account for the resale levy when you are purchasing a second subsidised flat to ensure that you have the necessary finances to carry out the transaction.

If you are taking up a bank loan, you have to pay 5% of the downpayment in cash. The remaining 20% can be paid using CPF savings.

There are other costs which have to be paid in cash:

- Renovation costs
- Your agent’s commission
- Option fees

Are you at the crossroads of choosing between an HDB housing loan or a bank loan for your flat purchase?

Learn the difference between an HDB loan and a bank loan before determining the best option that suits your needs.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
|  | **Bank loan** | **HDB housing loan** | 
| **Loan quantum** | You can borrow up to 75% of the flat purchase price if the loan period is 25 years and below | You can borrow up to 75% of the flat purchase price However, you will be required to use all of your Ordinary Account savings above $20,000 first | 
| **Downpayment and payment during key collection** | The minimum downpayment and payment during key collection required is 25% of the purchase price You may use your Ordinary Account savings for your downpayment However, 5% of it has to be paid for in cash | The minimum downpayment and payment during key collection required is 20% of the purchase price which can be fully paid for using your Ordinary Account savings | 
| **Use of CPF savings and previous property sales proceeds** | You may use or retain any amount in your Ordinary Account (up to applicable limits) | If you are taking a second HDB loan(up to applicable limits), you and the essential occupier need to use 50% of the cash proceeds from the disposal of the existing or last-owned HDB flat | 
| **Interest rates** | Bank interest rates fluctuate as these are more affected by the economic environment | The HDB interest rate is 0.1% above the Ordinary Account interest rate, which is currently 2.6% | 
| **Repayment amounts** | Fluctuates depending on loan interest rate | Relatively constant due to stable interest rate | 
| **Capital repayment or refinance loan** | Early and late repayment penalties may apply Penalties are subject to the terms and conditions of the loan provider May only refinance loan with banks and unable to refinance to HDB loan | There is no early repayment penalty, but a late payment charge of 7.5% per annum Option to refinance to bank loan |

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
There may be instances where you have to pay the downpayment for your next flat before you've received the sales proceeds from your existing flat. In such cases, there are schemes and bridging loans available.

HDB has schemes to facilitate the buying and selling process for existing flat owners.

- Enhanced Contra Facility
- Contra Payment Facility for new flats

Most people view the monies in their Ordinary Account as the main source to finance their home purchase. While it is true that CPF is an essential means to financing your home, it is important to balance the purchase of your dream home with your future needs. This is because your CPF savings will eventually become your retirement income.

Here are some considerations for using cash or CPF.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
| **Using cash** | **Using CPF** | 
| **Less flexibility for your other expenses** Using cash to pay for your home purchase/loan means less cash available for your other expenses. However, the unused CPF monies will contribute to your retirement sum. | **More flexibility for your other expenses** Using your CPF frees up your cash savings and allows you to use it for other expenses. | 
| **More stable returns on your savings for retirement and housing** The unused monies in your Ordinary Account can earn up to 3.5%\* risk-free interest. These Ordinary Account monies can also be a source of emergency fund for financing your flat in times of need or savings for your retirement. | **Less certainty on your savings for retirement and housing** While you can place the unused cash in various investment instruments and possibly earn a higher rate of return than the Ordinary Account, it is also possible to earn a lower rate of return or even make a loss. | 
| **Potentially higher cash proceeds upon sale** Using cash means that you will not need to make a CPF refund to your CPF account upon the sale of your property. Thus, you may receive higher cash proceeds. | **Possibly lower proceeds upon sale** You will need to refund more to your CPF account and thus may receive lower cash proceeds. Nonetheless, you can still use your CPF refund for your next flat, even though it cannot be used for payments that need to be paid in cash such as renovation. |

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
While using CPF to finance your home may provide more liquidity and flexibility in cash, you will lose out on earning the risk-free interest rates of up to 3.5%\* in your Ordinary Account for your savings on retirement and housing. Ultimately, do consider both your short term and long term needs before deciding which option is most suitable for you.

You can use CPF for the initial purchase of your home and subsequently use cash or a mix of both cash and CPF for your mortgage instalments.

Are you looking to buy a new or resale HDB flat? You may be looking to upgrade to a larger (and more costly) flat for a variety of reasons. While doing so, it is important to buy a flat within your financial means and also consider your retirement needs.

|  | **New Flat** | **Resale Flat** | 
| **Search, plan, contract** | Check eligibility to buy flat and grants available Search for desired area to live in upcoming flat launches | Register intent to buy Search for desired flat Negotiate with seller and request for Option to purchase (OTP) Choose mode of financing Request for value from HDB Exercise OTP | 
| **Application process** | Apply for flat online at HDB's website during sales launch or open booking Book a flat based on queue position Pay the option fee | Submit resale application Endorse resale documents Pay resale fees Obtain approval from HDB | 
| **Completion of sale** | 6 months after booking of flat, sign the Agreement for Lease Make downpayment When the flat is ready, collect the keys Pay balance purchase price | Attend completion appointment at HDB |

Do understand the sale process, so that you can plan and manage your timelines and smoothen the process.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
Having a good estimation of your sales proceeds can also help you make a more

informed decision when it comes to your next home purchase.

|  | **HDB flat** | **Others** | 
| **Plan, contract** | Register intent to sell on HDB's website Receive a preliminary assessment on your eligibility to sell your HDB flat Determine the selling price of your flat, list flat for sale, negotiate with buyers Grant Option to Purchase (OTP) to potential buyers | Doing paperwork and listing flat for sale Viewing and negotiations with buyer Grant OTP to potential buyers | 
| **Application process** | Buyer exercises OTP Buyer and seller to submit resale applications online within 7 days of each other Endorse resale documents Pay resale fees Obtain resale approval | Buyer exercises OTP Buyer signs Sale and Purchase agreement Buyer pays Buyer's Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (if any) | 
| **Completion of sale** | Attend completion appointment at HDB | Completion of sale upon full payment |

When you used your CPF savings for your property, your retirement savings are reduced. As such, upon the sale of your property, the sales proceeds will be used to pay off the outstanding housing loan taken to buy the property and refund the CPF amount used for your property and accrued interest, regardless of the Manner of Holding. This is to restore your retirement savings.

If you had pledged the property to make up your retirement sum, you will also need to refund the pledged amount.

As long as your property is sold at market value, you do not need to fork out additional cash to top up the shortfall if the sales proceeds are insufficient to refund the amount of CPF monies used with accrued interest, after paying the outstanding loan.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Non-mature Estates
content:
However, you are required to refund the option monies received to your co-owner’s and your own CPF savings as it forms part of the selling price of the flat.

The remaining sales proceeds after paying off the housing loan will be distributed based on the proportion of your principal amount used with accrued interest(P+I) to the total P+I of all owners.

The process for refunding your Ordinary Account monies differs whether you do so before or after 55.

Here’s what happens to your money after you sell your flat.

The type of ownership of your flat is termed as the Manner of Holding.

Under a joint tenancy, you and your co-owners will have an equal interest in the property.

While you and your co-owner can subsequently sell the entire property, you will need to convert to tenancy-in-common first to only sell your share of the property.

The right of survivorship also applies.

Under tenancy-in-common, each co-owner owns a separate share in the flat, with the total shares adding up to 100%.

The right of survivorship does not apply, meaning that upon the demise of an owner, his/her interest will be distributed according to his/her will (if any). In the absence of a will, it will be distributed in accordance with the Intestate Succession Act.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Joint tenancy
content: If you or your co-owners decide to sell your share of the property, you would need to convert the joint tenancy to a tenancy-in-common first.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Tenancy-in-common
content:
If you hold the property under tenancy-in-common, you are able to sell your share in the property.

Similar to a sale of the entire property, you will be also be required to refund the principal amount of CPF used and the accrued interest (P+I) based on your respective proportions.

You might need to fork out additional cash to refund to your CPF account if you use more CPF monies than your share of property. This is to ensure that CPF members who had used more CPF savings than their share of property will still have sufficient CPF savings for their retirement and housing needs.

When selling our flat, we tend to overlook the costs involved, and may overestimate our total proceeds received in cash. Besides paying off the outstanding home loan, we also have to refund the CPF principal amount used plus accrued interest, and to pay for expenses such as your agent's commission and sale-related administrative and legal fees. It is also possible not to have any cash proceeds despite selling your flat at a higher price!

Let's take a look from the context of John and Sarah to help us make a more informed choice when it comes to our own flat sale.

When John and Sarah got the keys to their HDB flat 5 years ago in 2017, they purchased it at $240,000. The breakdown of the costs is as follows:

| Initial flat purchase cost |  | 
|---|---|
| Purchase price | $240,000 | 
| Downpayment (10%) | $24,000 | 
| Loan taken (90% LTV) | $216,000 |

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Tenancy-in-common
content:
John and Sarah sold their flat at $520,000. Upon settling the outstanding loan, making the required CPF refunds and other costs involved, they received balance sales proceeds of $234,000. The breakdown is as follows:

| Selling transaction |  | 
|---|---|
| **Selling price\*** | **$520,000** | 
| -outstanding loan | - $183,000 | 
| - CPF refunds (principal amount used and accrued interest) | - $90,000 | 
| - other expenses related to sale (agent commission, admin and legal fees) | - $13,000 | 
| **= Balance sales proceeds** | **= $234,000** |

*\*Selling price includes the option monies received from buyer*

**When you pay your monthly instalments to HDB or banks, only the principal amount gets deducted from your outstanding loan balance. The interest is paid to HDB or banks for granting you the loan.**

In this case, you may notice that despite paying approximately $59,000\* in monthly instalments so far, only 56%($33,000/$59,000) goes towards paying off the principal amount. The remaining sum of $26,000 are interest expenses that do not reduce your overall loan balance.

Do take note of the above, so as to be more informed of where your monthly instalments are going to!

\*$59,000 is the sum of the total monthly instalments paid over 5 years, based on a HDB loan of $216,000 and a 25 year loan tenure

While upgrading your flat, it is important to ensure that your retirement needs are taken care of as well. While it may not be top of mind when buying your home, your housing purchase has a significant impact on your ability to pursue the purposeful retirement you are dreaming of.

Find out how you can ensure your retirement needs are not compromised while upgrading your flat.

section_heading: Home buying guide for members below 55 > Tenancy-in-common
content:
If you've used your Ordinary Account savings for your property, you are eligible to make a Voluntary Housing Refund.

The earlier you make a voluntary refund, the more interest you will earn to boost your CPF savings for retirement. In addition, you may receive more cash proceeds when you sell your property as you will need to refund a lesser amount to your CPF account.

Having more CPF savings will translate into higher or longer CPF payouts in your golden years.

After effecting the Voluntary Housing Refund, you can re-use your Ordinary Account savings for future housing needs too, ensuring the liquidity of your savings.

If you are taking an HDB loan, you can consider making a partial repayment and paying off your housing loan in advance to reduce your financial commitments. Doing so will help to shorten the repayment period, cutting down on the interest that you would need to pay. This can help to increase your savings and further grow your retirement income.

However, do be mindful if you are taking a bank loan as you may incur early repayment charges. Do check with HDB or your bank for more details.

There are a few means to increase your passive income and boost your retirement income while living in your flat. These include the Lease Buyback scheme, right-sizing or even renting out a room in your flat.

Explore if any of these options are viable for you!
